title.rhyme: Chapter 4: The Prince of Chenliu crown'd as Han's lord; His strike undone, Cao Cao presents the sword.
title.prose: Chapter 4: The Han Emperor is deposed and the Prince of Chenliu made sovereign; plotting against Dong the traitor, Mengde presents a sword.
title.original: 第四回：廢漢帝陳留為皇，謀董賊孟德獻刀

paragraphs.original: 且說董卓欲殺袁紹，李儒止之曰：「事未可定，不可妄殺。」袁紹手提寶劍，辭別百官而出，懸節東門，奔翼州去了。卓謂太傳袁隗曰：「汝姪無禮，吾看汝面，姑恕之。廢立之事若何？」隗曰：「太尉所見是也。」卓曰：「敢有阻大議者，以軍法從事。」群臣震恐，皆云：「一聽尊命。」宴罷，卓問侍中周毖、校尉伍瓊曰：「袁紹此去若何？」周毖曰：「袁紹忿忿而去，若購之急，勢必為變，且袁氏樹恩四世，門生故吏，遍於天下；倘收豪傑以聚徙眾，英雄因之而起，山東非公有也。不如赦之，拜為一郡守，則紹喜於免罪，必無患矣。」伍瓊曰：「袁紹好謀無斷，不足為慮；誠不若加之一郡守，以收民心。」
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of Dong Zhuo, who would have slain Yuan Shao; but Li Ru stayed him, saying, 'The matter is not yet decided — you must not slay rashly.' Yuan Shao, with his treasured sword in hand, took leave of the hundred officials and went forth; he hung up his ensign at the East Gate, and fled to Jizhou. Zhuo said to the Grand Tutor Yuan Wei, 'Your nephew has been discourteous; out of regard for your face, I shall pardon him for the present. As for the matter of deposition and installation — what say you?' Wei said, 'What Your Excellency the Grand Commandant has perceived is right.' Zhuo said, 'Whoever dares obstruct this great design shall be dealt with by military law.' The assembled ministers were stricken with fear, and all said, 'In all things we obey your honored command.' When the banquet had ended, Zhuo asked the Palace Attendant Zhou Bi and the Colonel Wu Qiong, 'How shall it be with Yuan Shao now that he has departed?' Zhou Bi said, 'Yuan Shao has departed in fury; should he be hunted in haste, the matter must surely turn to disorder. Moreover, the house of Yuan has planted favors for four generations: their disciples and former subordinates are spread throughout the realm. Should he gather men of valor and assemble a following, heroes would rise on his account, and the lands east of the mountains would no longer be Your Lordship's. Better to pardon him and appoint him Grand Administrator of a single commandery: Shao will rejoice at being spared from punishment, and there will surely be no further trouble.' Wu Qiong said, 'Yuan Shao is fond of plots but lacking in resolve; he is not worth great concern. It would truly be best to invest him as Grand Administrator of a commandery, and so to win the hearts of the people.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) would slay [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao); but [Li Ru](char-li-ru) spake:
'The matter is not fix'd — no rash blow take.'
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), with sword in hand, took leave that day,
Hung up his seal at East Gate, fled away
To [Jizhou](loc-ji-province). Then to [Wei](char-yuan-wei), the Tutor Grand,
Said [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): 'Thy nephew rudely scorn'd our hand;
For thy sake I forgive. As for the throne,
What of our great design? Make thy view known.'
[Wei](char-yuan-wei): 'What the Grand Commandant sees is right.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): 'Who blocks the change shall meet the sword's bite.'
The lords with one accord, in fear, did vow:
'In all things, Lord, to thy command we bow.'
The banquet done, [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) ask'd Zhou Bi and Qiong:
'Where bends [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)? What course will he prolong?'
Said Bi: 'In wrath hath [Shao](char-yuan-shao) depart'd hence:
If close pursu'd, he'll rise to thy expense.
For four whole reigns the Yuans have planted grace,
Their clients fill the realm in every place.
If heroes gather round his rising sign,
The east of mountains slips beyond thy line.
Far better pardon, with a comm'ndery's seat:
Glad to be spar'd, no further harm we'll meet.'
Wu Qiong said: '[Shao](char-yuan-shao) schemes, but need not wake thy fear;
Grant him a post, and draw the people near.'

paragraphs.original: 卓從之，即日差人拜紹為渤海太守。九月朔，請帝陞嘉德殿，大會文武。卓拔劍在手，對眾曰：「天子闇弱，不足以君天下。今有策文一道，宜為宣讀。」乃令李儒讀策曰：「孝靈皇帝，早棄臣民；皇帝，海內仰望。而帝天資輕佻，威儀不恪，居喪慢惰：否德既彰，有忝大位。皇太后教無母儀，統政荒亂。永樂太后暴崩，眾論惑焉。三綱之道，天地之紀，毋乃有闕？陳留王協，聖德偉懋，規矩肅然；居喪哀戚，言不以邪；休聲美譽，天下所聞：宜承洪業，為萬世統。茲廢皇帝為弘農王，皇太后還政。請奉陳留王為皇帝，應天順人，以慰生靈之望。」
paragraphs.prose: Zhuo followed his counsel, and that very same day dispatched a man to invest Shao as Grand Administrator of Bohai. On the first day of the ninth month, the Emperor was bidden to ascend the Jiade Hall, where there was held a grand assembly of civil and military officials. Zhuo, sword drawn and held in his hand, addressed the assembly: 'The Son of Heaven is dim and weak, and is not equal to lordship over the empire. There is here a written decree which ought now to be proclaimed.' Thereupon he ordered Li Ru to read the decree, which said: 'The Filial Emperor Ling early forsook his subjects and people; on the present Emperor were the eyes of all within the seas. Yet the Emperor is, in his nature, frivolous and light, lacking gravity in his demeanor, slothful and idle in his mourning: ill virtue is now plainly manifest, and he is unworthy of the great seat. The Empress Dowager, in her teaching, has shown no maternal example, and her governance is in disorder. The Empress Dowager Yongle died of a sudden, and the speech of the multitude was thereby perplexed. The way of the Three Bonds, the framework of Heaven and Earth — are these not fallen short? The Prince of Chenliu, Xie — his sage virtue is great and abounding; in deportment he is grave and proper; in mourning he sorrows and grieves; in his speech is no crookedness; his fair fame and reputation are heard throughout the realm: he ought to inherit the great work, and be the line for ten thousand generations. Therefore: the Emperor is deposed as Prince of Hongnong; the Empress Dowager shall return the government. We pray that the Prince of Chenliu be revered as Emperor, in answer to Heaven and in accord with men, to comfort the hopes of all living beings.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) took advice, and on that very day
Made [Shao](char-yuan-shao) [Bohai](loc-bohai)'s chief lord without delay.
The ninth moon's first — the [Emperor](char-prince-bian) was led
To Jiade Hall, where lords of all rank spread.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) drew his sword, and to the assembly cri'd:
'The [Sovereign](char-prince-bian)'s dim — unfit our realm to guide.
A writ here speaks: let now its words appear.'
Then [Li Ru](char-li-ru) read: 'The Filial [Ling](char-emperor-ling), austere,
His subjects and his folk too soon forsook;
To his successor turn'd the empire's look —
Yet light his nature, gravity undone;
In mourning slack, his idle hours have run.
Ill virtue plain — the seat of state's a shame;
The [Empress Mother](char-empress-he) strays from mother's name;
Her rule lies wild; the [Empress Yongle](char-empress-dowager-dong) dy'd
Of sudden death; the realm in murmurs ply'd.
The Three great Bonds and Heaven-Earth's design,
Are these not lapsed, no longer well-aligned?
But [Chenliu's prince](char-prince-xie), of holy virtue's height,
With grave deportment, mourning sad and right,
With speech of no crook'd word, and fair acclaim
Throughout the empire heard, beyond all blame:
Let him receive the throne, the line uphold
For ages ten-times-thousand to be told.
Therefore, deposed the [Sovereign](char-prince-bian): Hongnong now
He shall be styl'd; the [Empress](char-empress-he) lay her brow
Of rule aside. We pray [Chenliu](char-prince-xie) the throne
Embrace, by Heaven's will and people's own.'

paragraphs.original: 李儒讀策畢，卓叱左右扶帝下殿，解其璽綬，北面長跪，稱臣聽命。又呼太后去服候敕。帝后皆號哭。群臣無不悲慘。階下一大臣，憤怒高叫曰：「賊臣董卓，敢為欺天之謀，吾當以頸血濺之！」揮手中象簡，直擊董卓。卓大怒，喝武士拏下，乃尚書丁管也。卓命牽出斬也。管罵不絕口，至死神色不變。後人有詩歎曰：董賊潛懷廢立圖，漢家宗社委丘墟。滿朝臣宰皆囊括，惟有丁公是丈夫。
paragraphs.prose: When Li Ru had finished reading the decree, Zhuo shouted at the attendants to assist the Emperor in descending from the dais; they took from him his seal and ribbon, and made him kneel long facing the north, declaring himself a subject and awaiting command. He further called upon the Empress Dowager to put off her regalia and await orders. Emperor and Empress alike wailed aloud; among the assembled ministers, there was none not stricken with grief. From below the steps, a great minister cried out in fury: 'Traitorous minister Dong Zhuo — thou darest contrive a design that affronts Heaven; I shall splash thee with the blood of my own neck!' And waving the ivory tablet in his hand, he struck straight at Dong Zhuo. Zhuo, in great wrath, shouted to his warriors to seize the man and bring him down: it was the Imperial Secretary Ding Guan. Zhuo ordered him led out and beheaded. Guan railed without ceasing, and his countenance remained unchanged till his death. A later poet sighed of him in verse, saying: 'Dong the traitor secretly cherished a plan to depose and install; / The Han ancestral altars were given over to ruined heaps. / The whole assembly of ministers were all swept along; / There was only Lord Ding, who was a true man indeed.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Li Ru](char-li-ru) concluded; [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) with stern commands
Bade men to lead the [Emp'ror](char-prince-bian) down the stands.
They took his seal-and-ribbon from his hand,
And to the north he knelt, where subjects stand.
The [Empress Mother](char-empress-he) too her robes laid down,
Awaiting orders' fall, deprived of crown.
The [Emp'ror](char-prince-bian) and his consort wept aloud;
And every minister with sorrow bow'd.
Beneath the steps, in fury, one out-cri'd:
'Traitor [Dong](char-dong-zhuo), Heaven's law thou dost deride,
My neck's own blood shall splash thee, ere I bow!'
He rais'd his tablet, struck him on the brow.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), wroth, bade warriors hale him forth to die.
'Twas Sec'try Ding, who held a fearless eye.
He curs'd unceasing till the fatal blow,
His countenance unchang'd, no fear did show.
A later poet sigh'd, his deed to frame,
And in these lines preserv'd his honor'd name:
'[Dong](char-dong-zhuo), traitor, secret cherish'd plot of throne;
The Han ancestral hearths to ruin grown.
The whole court's ministers, in silence bound;
Lord Ding alone — true manhood here was found.'

paragraphs.original: 卓請陳留王登殿。群臣朝賀畢，卓命扶何太后并弘農王及帝妃唐氏於永安宮閒住，封鎖宮門，禁群臣無得擅入。可憐少帝四月登基，至九月即被廢。卓所立陳留王協，表字伯和，靈帝中子，即獻帝也，時年九歲。改元初平。董卓為相國，贊拜不名，入朝不趨，劍履上殿，威福莫比。李儒勸卓擢用名流，以收人望，因薦蔡邕之才。卓命徵之，邕不赴。卓怒，使人謂邕曰：「如不來，當滅汝族。」邕懼，只得應命而至。卓見邕大喜，一月三遷其官，拜為侍中，甚見親厚。
paragraphs.prose: Zhuo invited the Prince of Chenliu to ascend the throne. When the ministers had finished paying their court greetings, Zhuo ordered that the Empress Dowager He, together with the Prince of Hongnong and the Emperor's consort Lady Tang, be conveyed to the Yong'an Palace, there to dwell at leisure; and the gates of the palace were sealed and locked, the ministers forbidden to enter at will. Pitiable was the young Emperor, who had ascended in the fourth month and was deposed by the ninth. The Prince of Chenliu whom Zhuo set up — Xie, courtesy Bohe, second son of Emperor Ling — that is the Emperor Xian; he was at that time nine years of age. The era was changed to Chuping. Dong Zhuo took the office of Chancellor of State; in court he was announced without his name, did not hasten as he entered the audience, and ascended the hall with sword and shoes; in majesty and bounty none could compare with him. Li Ru urged Zhuo to promote men of repute, that he might gather popular esteem, and so recommended the talents of Cai Yong. Zhuo ordered him summoned, but Yong did not come. Zhuo, in anger, sent a man to tell Yong: 'If thou come not, thy clan shall be exterminated.' Yong, in fear, had no choice but to obey the summons and arrive. Zhuo, on seeing Yong, was greatly pleased, and in one month thrice promoted his office, appointing him Palace Attendant; and showed him much intimacy and kindness.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) bade [Chenliu](char-prince-xie) the throne ascend on high;
The ministers paid homage with one cry.
The [Empress He](char-empress-he), the [Hongnong Prince](char-prince-bian), and [Tang](char-lady-tang)
To Yong'an Palace went; the gates' bolt rang.
The lords were barr'd from entering at all;
Poor king! Whose throne so swiftly came to fall:
He mounted in the fourth moon, throne to wear;
By ninth he was depos'd, beyond repair.
The new-set prince, [Xie](char-prince-xie), son of [Ling](char-emperor-ling) the late,
Nine years of age — and [Xian](char-prince-xie) his name of state.
The era new — [Chuping](misc-chuping) was now its claim;
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), as Chancellor, no peer could name.
Announc'd uncall'd by name, his pace unrush'd,
With sword on hip and shoes the dais brush'd.
[Li Ru](char-li-ru) urg'd [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): 'Draw famous men, that they
The realm's good will to thee may bend and stay.'
Then nam'd [Cai Yong](char-cai-yong), of talent bright and rare;
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) summon'd; [Yong](char-cai-yong) refus'd to enter there.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), wroth, sent word: 'If thou come not in haste,
Thy kindred clan shall to extinction wast'.'
[Yong](char-cai-yong), fearful, came. [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) welcom'd him with grace;
Thrice rais'd his office in a month's brief space.
Made him Attendant, kept him near at hand,
And much esteem'd him 'midst his closest band.

paragraphs.original: 卻說少帝與何太后、唐妃困於永安宮中，衣服飲食，漸漸欠缺；少帝淚不曾乾。一日，偶見雙燕飛於庭中，遂吟詩一首。詩曰：嫩草綠凝煙，裊裊雙飛燕。洛水一條青，陌上人稱羨。　遠望碧雲深，是吾舊宮殿。何人仗忠義，洩我心中怨！
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of the young Emperor, with the Empress Dowager He and Consort Tang, confined in the Yong'an Palace; their clothing and food grew gradually wanting, and the young Emperor's tears were never dry. One day, by chance he saw a pair of swallows flying within the courtyard, and so chanted a poem. The poem said: 'Tender grass green, gathered as if in mist; / Wavering and slender, two swallows fly in pair. / The Luo River, a single thread of blue; / Men on the road look on with envy. / Far away I gaze on the deep azure clouds — / It is my own old palace. / Who shall bear up loyalty and righteousness, / And vent the resentment of my heart?'
paragraphs.rhyme:
Now in Yong'an the [young King](char-prince-bian) close restrain'd,
With [Empress He](char-empress-he) and [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang) detain'd,
Their robes and food by stages thinner grew;
The [young King](char-prince-bian)'s tears, like rain, would not subdue.
One day, by chance, two swallows cross'd his eye;
He chanted forth this verse, with mournful sigh:
'The tender grass, in green and misty fold,
Two swallows fluttering soft I do behold.
The Luo, blue thread, runs straight upon the plain;
Where men along the road in envy strain.
Far off I gaze where azure clouds lie deep,
There stand my ancient halls, beyond my keep.
Who'll stand for loyalty and righteous claim,
And vent the grievance harbour'd in my frame?'

paragraphs.original: 董卓時常使人探聽。是日獲得此詩，來呈董卓。卓曰：「怨望作詩，殺之有名矣。」遂命李儒帶武士十人，入宮弒帝。帝與后、妃正在樓上，宮女報李儒至，帝大驚。儒以鴆酒奉帝，帝問何故。儒曰：「春日融和，董相國特上壽酒。」太后曰：「既云壽酒，汝可先飲。」儒怒曰：「汝不飲耶？」呼左右持短刀白練於前曰：「壽酒不飲，可領此二物！」唐妃跪告曰：「妾身代帝飲酒，願公存母子性命。」儒叱曰：「汝何人，可代王死？」乃舉酒與何太后曰：「汝可先飲！」后大罵何進無謀，引賊入京，致有今日之禍。儒催逼帝，帝曰：「容我與太后作別。」乃大慟而作歌。其歌曰：天地易兮日月翻，棄萬乘兮退守藩。為巨逼兮命不久，大勢去兮空淚潸！
paragraphs.prose: Dong Zhuo had men constantly on the watch. That day they obtained this poem and brought it to Zhuo. Zhuo said: 'Composing a poem of resentment — here is good cause to put him to death.' He thereupon ordered Li Ru, with ten armed men, to enter the palace and assassinate the Emperor. The Emperor, with the Empress Dowager and Consort Tang, was at that moment in the upper chamber, when a palace maid reported the coming of Li Ru, and the Emperor was greatly startled. Ru offered him a cup of poisoned wine; the Emperor asked the reason. Ru said: 'The spring day is mild and warm; Chancellor of State Dong has specially sent up this wine for Your Majesty's long life.' The Empress Dowager said: 'If it is wine of long life, you may drink first.' Ru, in anger, said: 'Will you not drink?' He called for attendants to come forward with a short blade and a length of white silk, saying: 'If you will not drink the long-life wine, then take these two things instead!' Consort Tang knelt and pleaded: 'Let me drink the wine in His Majesty's stead, and may you spare the lives of mother and son.' Ru rebuked her: 'Who art thou, to die for the King?' He then took up the wine and offered it to Empress Dowager He, saying: 'You may drink first!' The Empress Dowager loudly cursed He Jin for his lack of strategy, who had brought the bandits into the capital, and so brought about this calamity. Ru pressed the Emperor; the Emperor said: 'Suffer me to take leave of the Empress Dowager.' Then in deep grief he composed a song. The song ran: 'Heaven and earth are altered; sun and moon have turned; / I cast off the myriad chariots, retreating to my vassal-state. / By a giant pressed, my life shall not be long: / the great tide is gone — in vain do my tears flow!'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) had spies that listen'd, day and night;
That day they bore the poem to his sight.
Said [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): 'A poem of grievance — pretext clear
To slay the [King](char-prince-bian).' He bade [Li Ru](char-li-ru) appear
With ten arm'd men in train; the palace's way
They enter'd, that the [King](char-prince-bian) might fall their prey.
Above, the [Empress](char-empress-he), [Tang](char-lady-tang), and [Sovereign](char-prince-bian) — three,
Sat in the upper hall in privacy.
A maid announc'd [Li Ru](char-li-ru)'s approach; the [King](char-prince-bian)
Was startled, fear'd what such a call might bring.
[Ru](char-li-ru) proffer'd up a cup of poison'd wine;
The [King](char-prince-bian) ask'd why. Said [Ru](char-li-ru): 'The day is fine
Of spring; the Chancellor of State doth send
This long-life cup, that [Sovereign](char-prince-bian)'s days extend.'
The [Empress](char-empress-he): 'Long-life wine? Then drink thou first,
That we may witness 'tis no draught accurs'd.'
[Ru](char-li-ru), wroth, retorted: 'Wilt thou drink it not?'
And bade attendants forth — they swiftly brought
A short blade and a length of silk-band white:
'Refuse the cup — these two shall be thy plight!'
Then [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang) knelt low, in fervent plea:
'In [Sovereign](char-prince-bian)'s stead, the cup pray pass to me!
Preserve the mother and the kingly son.'
[Ru](char-li-ru) chid: 'Who art thou? Die for king? Have done!'
He turn'd, the wine to [Empress He](char-empress-he) convey'd:
'Drink first!' — She loud [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s blind plan inveigh'd,
That brought the bandit-troop into the gate,
And wrought today this woeful turn of state.
[Ru](char-li-ru) press'd; the [King](char-prince-bian): 'A moment, ere I die,
Take leave of her, my mother.' With a sigh,
Deep grief broke forth in song; his parting strain
He sang — the [Emperor](char-prince-bian)'s dirge, in tones of pain:
'Earth, heaven turn; the sun and moon awry,
Ten thousand chariots cast — to vassal lie
Confin'd. By giant's pow'r my days grow few;
The tide is gone — my tears in stream renew.'

paragraphs.original: 唐妃亦作歌曰：皇天將崩兮，后土頹﹔身為帝姬兮，恨不隨。生死異路兮，從此別﹔奈何煢速兮，心中悲！
paragraphs.prose: Consort Tang too composed a song, saying: 'Imperial Heaven is about to fall; Sovereign Earth totters! Born a consort to the Emperor, I lament that I cannot follow him. Life and death are different paths; from this day forth we are parted. Alas, alone and swift — sorrow within my heart!'
paragraphs.rhyme:
Then [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang) gave forth her parting strain:
'Imperial Heaven falls; Earth crumbles plain.
Born Consort to the [King](char-prince-bian) — I lament in vain
That I may not attend him on his train.
Life-death lie sunder'd; from this hour we part;
Alas, alone and swift — grief in my heart!'

paragraphs.original: 歌罷，相抱而哭。李儒叱曰：「相國立等回報，汝等俄延，望誰救耶？」太后大罵：「董賊逼我母子，皇天不佑！汝等助惡，必當滅族！」儒大怒，雙手扯住太后，直攛下樓，叱武士絞死唐妃，以鴆酒灌殺少帝，還報董卓。卓命葬於城外。自此每夜入宮，姦淫宮女，夜宿龍床。嘗引軍出城，行到陽城地方，時當二月，村民社賽。男女皆集，卓命軍士圍住，盡皆殺之，掠婦女財物，裝載車上，懸頭千餘顆於車下，連軫還都，揚言殺賊大勝而回；於城門下焚燒人頭，以婦女財物分散眾軍。
paragraphs.prose: The song being done, they embraced one another and wept. Li Ru rebuked them: 'The Chancellor of State awaits my report; you delay — whose rescue do you hope for?' The Empress Dowager loudly cursed: 'Dong the traitor presses my mother and son! Heaven shall not aid him! You who aid the evil — your clan must surely be exterminated!' Li Ru, in great wrath, with both hands seized the Empress Dowager and thrust her down from the upper chamber; he ordered the warriors to strangle Consort Tang to death; with the poisoned wine he forced the young Emperor to drink, and so killed him. He returned and reported to Dong Zhuo. Zhuo ordered them buried outside the city. From this time on, every night Zhuo entered the palace, defiled the palace maids, and slept upon the Dragon Bed. Once he led his troops out of the capital, and came to the region of Yangcheng. It was the second month, when the villagers held their spring festival of the Earth Altar; men and women had all gathered. Zhuo ordered his soldiers to surround them, and killed every one; they seized the women and the goods, loaded them onto carts, and hung over a thousand heads beneath the carts. They returned in column to the capital, proclaiming that they had won a great victory over the rebels. At the city gates they burned the heads, and distributed the women and the goods among the troops.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The song now done, in sorrowing embrace
They wept aloud. [Li Ru](char-li-ru)'s voice broke the place:
'The Chancellor of State waits for report!
Why linger ye? Whose rescue do ye court?'
The [Empress](char-empress-he) curs'd: 'That traitor doth oppress
Both me and son — may Heaven not him bless!
Ye who his evil serve — your clan shall fall;
Root and branch, destruction shall reach you all!'
[Ru](char-li-ru), wroth, with both hands seiz'd the [Empress](char-empress-he), tore
Her from the upper chamber to the floor.
He bade his men strangle [Lady Tang](char-lady-tang) outright;
The poison'd wine snuff'd out the [young King](char-prince-bian)'s light.
Then back to [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), his report [Ru](char-li-ru) did bear;
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) bade them buried beyond the city's air.
From that hour [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) each night the palace gain'd;
The maids he forc'd, the Dragon-Bed profan'd.
Once forth he march'd his troops without the gate,
To Yangcheng's bounds in second moon's full state.
An Earth-rite feast had drawn both man and maid;
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) bade his soldiers ring them, blade by blade,
And slaughter all. The women and the spoil
Were carted off, in plunder's heavy toil;
Beneath the carts a thousand heads were strung;
They march'd back column'd; loud the boast they sung:
'Great victory! The rebels we have slain!'
Beneath the city gates the heads burn'd plain;
The women and the goods he shar'd among
His troops, in bloody plunder loud and long.

paragraphs.original: 越騎校尉伍孚，字德瑜，見卓殘暴，憤恨不平。嘗於朝服內披小鎧，藏短刀，欲伺便殺卓。一日，卓入朝，孚迎至閣下，拔刀直刺卓。卓氣力大，兩手摳住；呂布便入，揪倒伍孚。卓問曰：「誰教汝反？」孚瞪目大喝曰：「汝非吾君，吾非汝臣，何反之有？汝罪惡盈天，人人願得而誅之！吾恨不車裂汝以謝天下！」卓大怒，命牽出剖剮之。孚至死罵不絕口。後人有詩讚之曰：漢末忠臣說伍孚，沖天豪氣世間無。朝堂殺賊名猶在，萬古堪稱大丈夫！
paragraphs.prose: At that time the Yuechi Cavalry Colonel Wu Fu, courtesy name Deyu, seeing the cruelty of Dong Zhuo, was filled with indignation. He had once worn a small set of armor beneath his court robes, with a short knife concealed, and waited an opportunity to slay Zhuo. One day, when Zhuo had come to court, Wu Fu met him at the entrance of the hall, drew his knife, and stabbed straight at Zhuo. But Zhuo's strength was great; with both hands he caught hold of him. Lü Bu came in just then, and threw Wu Fu to the ground. Zhuo asked: 'Who taught thee to rebel?' Wu Fu, with eyes wide and a great shout, said: 'Thou art not my lord, and I am not thy servant — what rebellion is here? Thy crimes fill heaven; every man longs to put thee to death! I lament that I could not have torn thee asunder by the chariot, to apologize to the realm!' Zhuo, in great rage, ordered him taken forth and cut to pieces. Wu Fu cursed without ceasing till his death. A later poet wrote a poem in his praise, saying: 'Wu Fu, called the loyal minister of Han's last days; / Heroic spirit piercing heaven, unmatched in all the world. / Slaying the traitor at court — his name endures still; / For ten thousand ages, he may be called a true man!'
paragraphs.rhyme:
Wu Fu, Yuechi Cavalry-Colonel hight,
Of style Deyu, beheld [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s might
Of cruelty, and was indignant sore.
Beneath his court-robe small armor he wore,
And in his sleeve a short knife hid for chance
To slay the tyrant. On a day, by hap,
When [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) to court had come, Fu met him by
The hall, drew forth his knife, and stabb'd full nigh.
But [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) had giant's strength: with both hands hold
He gripp'd Fu's wrists, and held him fast and bold.
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) burst in, and dash'd Wu Fu to ground.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): 'Who taught thee to rebel? Speak, traitor bound!'
Fu, wide-eyed, shouted: 'Thou art not my lord;
Nor I thy man — what rebel-act or word?
Thy crimes fill heaven; every man doth long
To see thee dead — and none could call it wrong!
My grief: I could not, by the chariot's wheel,
Have rent thee, all the realm's relief to seal!'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), wroth, bade lead him forth, in pieces small
To hew. Fu curs'd unceasing till his fall.
A later poet prais'd him in a lay:
'Wu Fu, of Han's last days, the loyal stay;
His soaring spirit pierc'd the heavens through,
None in the world hath match'd his ardour true.
Within the court the traitor-slayer's name
Endures; for ages, true man's lasting fame.'

paragraphs.original: 董卓自此出入常帶甲士護衛。時袁紹在渤海，聞知董卓弄權，乃差人齎密書來見王允。書略曰：卓賊欺天廢主，人不忍言；而公恣其跋扈，如不聽聞，豈報國效忠之臣哉？紹今集兵練卒，欲掃清王室，未敢輕動。公若有心，當乘間圖之。若有驅使，即當奉命。
paragraphs.prose: From this time, Dong Zhuo's comings and goings were always attended by armored guards. At that time Yuan Shao, in Bohai, hearing that Dong Zhuo was abusing power, sent a man with a secret letter to Wang Yun. The letter ran in summary: 'The traitor Zhuo deceives Heaven and deposes the sovereign, in a manner men cannot bear to speak of; and you, sir, suffer his arrogance, as though you heard it not — are you a minister loyal in repaying his country? Shao now is mustering troops and drilling soldiers, wishing to sweep clean the royal house, but dares not move lightly. If you, sir, have the heart, you should seize the opportunity to plot against him. Should you have any orders for me, I shall obey at once.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
From this hour [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) went to and fro
With armèd men attending, friend or foe.
Now [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) at [Bohai](loc-bohai), who had heard
Of [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s abuse of power, sent a word
By secret letter unto [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun)'s hand;
Whose burden ran: 'The traitor mocks the land
Of Heaven, hath depos'd our lawful king,
No tongue can suffer such a deed to sing.
And you, my Lord, his arrogance endure,
As if not hearing — call you this the sure
True mark of loyal minister to state?
[Shao](char-yuan-shao) now is gathering arms, by steady weight
Drilling his men, to cleanse the royal house;
But dares not move too lightly, lest he rouse
The watching hand. Hast thou the heart, then plot
Thou his undoing — seize the timely lot.
And shouldst thou send command, I'll come straightway
And bend my force to all that thou shalt say.'

paragraphs.original: 王允得書，尋思無計。一日，於侍班閣子內見舊臣俱在，允曰：「今日老夫賤降，晚間敢屈眾位到舍小酌。」眾官皆曰：「必來祝壽。」當晚王允設宴後堂，公卿皆至。酒行數巡，王允忽然掩面大哭。眾官驚問曰：「司徒貴誕，何故發悲？」允曰：「今日並非賤降，因欲與眾位一敘，恐董卓見疑，故託言耳。董卓欺主弄權，社稷旦夕難保。想高皇誅秦滅楚，奄有天下；誰想傳至今日，乃喪於董卓之手：此吾所以哭也。」於是眾官皆哭。坐中一人撫掌大笑曰：「滿朝公卿，夜哭到明，明哭到夜，還能哭死董卓否？」允視之，乃驍騎校尉曹操也。允怒曰：「汝祖宗亦食祿漢朝，今不思報國而反笑耶？」操曰：「吾非笑別事，笑眾位無一計殺董卓耳。操雖不才，願即斷董卓頭，懸之都門，以謝天下。」允避席問曰：「孟德有何高見？」操曰：「近日操屈身以事卓者，實欲乘間圖之耳。今卓頗信操，操因得時近卓。聞司徒有七星寶刀一口，願借與操入相府刺殺之，雖死不恨！」允曰：「孟德果有是心，天下幸甚！」遂親自酌酒奉操。操瀝酒設誓，允隨取寶刀與之。操藏刀，飲酒畢，即起身辭別眾官而去。眾官又坐了一回，亦俱散訖。
paragraphs.prose: Wang Yun received the letter, and pondered the matter, but could find no plan. One day, in the chamber of attending ministers, he saw the old officials all assembled, and Yun said, 'Today is the humble anniversary of my birth; this evening I dare beg you all to come to my house for a small cup of wine.' The officials all said, 'We shall surely come to wish your longevity.' That evening Wang Yun set a banquet in the rear hall, and the dukes and lords all arrived. After the wine had gone several rounds, Wang Yun suddenly covered his face and wept aloud. The officials, startled, asked, 'Minister of the Masses, on the day of your honored birth, why this grief?' Yun said, 'Today is not in truth my birthday; I wished to gather with you all, yet feared lest Dong Zhuo grow suspicious, and so used a pretext. Dong Zhuo deceives the sovereign and abuses power; the altars of state may not be preserved from morning till evening. Think how Gaozu slew Qin and destroyed Chu, and so encompassed all the realm; who would have thought that, passing down to this day, it should perish in the hand of Dong Zhuo? This is why I weep.' At this, all the officials wept. One man in the seat clapped his hands and laughed loud, saying, 'All you dukes and lords of the court, weeping from night till dawn, from dawn till night — can you yet weep Dong Zhuo to death?' Yun looked, and it was the Xiaoji Cavalry Colonel Cao Cao. Yun, in anger, said, 'Thy forebears too ate the salary of the Han court; now thou thinkest not to repay the country, but laughest instead?' Cao said, 'I do not laugh at any other thing — I laugh that none among you all has any plan to slay Dong Zhuo. Though I am unworthy, I am willing this very moment to cut off Dong Zhuo's head and hang it at the gate of the capital, to apologize to the realm.' Yun rose from his seat and asked, 'Mengde, what high counsel have you?' Cao said, 'In recent days I have lowered myself to serve Zhuo only because I wished to seize an opportunity and plot against him. Now Zhuo trusts me well, and I have means to come near him at any time. I hear that you, Minister of the Masses, possess a Seven-Star Precious Sword; I beg to borrow it and enter the Chancellor's mansion to assassinate him — though I should die, I shall not regret!' Yun said, 'If Mengde truly has this heart, the realm is most fortunate!' Then he himself poured wine and offered it to Cao. Cao poured a libation of wine and swore his oath, and Yun thereupon took out the precious sword and gave it to him. Cao concealed the sword, finished his wine, and rose to take leave of the officials and depart. The officials sat a while longer, then likewise dispersed.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun), the letter read, no plan he found.
One day, where senior ministers stood round
The waiting hall, he spoke to those at hand:
'My humble birthday falls; pray come and stand
With me this eve, and share a modest cup.'
They said: 'We'll surely come, thy years to sup
And toast.' That night [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) within the rear
Hall set the feast; the dukes and lords drew near.
The wine had pass'd a few brief rounds, when, lo!
[Yun](char-wang-yun) veil'd his face, and tears began to flow.
The startl'd guests inquir'd: 'Excellence, why
On this thy honor'd birth-feast dost thou cry?'
[Yun](char-wang-yun) said: 'No birthday this — I form'd a tale
To gather you, lest [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s suspicion sail.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) deceives the king, abuses pow'r;
The state's foundations totter every hour.
Recall how [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu), of imperial hand,
Slew Qin, destroy'd the Chu, and rul'd the land
Beneath one sway. Who could have ever thought
That down to us his lineage would be brought
To perish in [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s grasp at last?
This is my grief; for this my tears flow fast.'
At this, the courtiers wept with [Yun](char-wang-yun), in pain.
But one mid-feast clapp'd hands and laugh'd amain:
'Ye dukes and lords of court, ye weep all day,
And weep all night — yet shall such weeping slay
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), with all his harsh and brutal might?'
[Yun](char-wang-yun) saw 'twas [Cao](char-cao-cao), Xiaoji-Colonel hight.
[Yun](char-wang-yun), wroth: 'Thy fathers ate the Han court's pay;
Now wilt thou not repay it — laugh'st, this day?'
[Cao](char-cao-cao) said: 'I laugh at nothing else, but this,
That none of you can plot [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s dismiss.
Though small my talent, I would seize his head
And on the city's gate hang up the dead,
To give the realm redress.' [Yun](char-wang-yun) left his seat:
'[Mengde](char-cao-cao), what plan hast thou? Speak, I entreat.'
[Cao](char-cao-cao): 'Late I bow'd to serve, with this intent:
To watch the moment, and his fall foment.
He trusts me well; my stay is near his side.
I hear, Excellence, in thy chamber bide
A Seven-Star Sword: lend it me — I'll go
To [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s own mansion, there to strike the blow.
Though I should die, no regret shall I know!'
[Yun](char-wang-yun): 'If thy heart be such, the realm is bless'd!'
Himself he pour'd the wine, and [Cao](char-cao-cao) address'd
With cup in hand. [Cao](char-cao-cao) spilt the libation,
Swore solemn oath; [Yun](char-wang-yun), in confirmation,
Took out the sword, and gave it him. The blade
Conceal'd, his cup well-drain'd, no longer stay'd,
[Cao](char-cao-cao) rose, took leave, and forth without delay.
The rest sat on awhile, then went their way.

paragraphs.original: 次日，曹操佩著寶刀，來至相府，問丞相何在。從人云：「在小閣中。」操竟入。見董卓坐於床上，呂布侍立於側。卓曰：「孟德來何遲？」操曰：「馬贏行遲耳。」卓顧謂布曰：「吾有西涼進來好馬，奉先可親去揀一騎賜與孟德。」布領令而去。操暗忖曰：「此賊合死！」即欲拔刀刺之。懼卓力大，未敢輕動。卓胖大不耐久坐，遂倒身而臥，轉面向內。操又思曰：「此賊當休矣！」急掣寶刀在手。恰待要刺，不想董卓仰面看衣鏡中，照見曹操在背後拔刀，急回身問曰：「孟德何為？」
paragraphs.prose: The next day, Cao Cao wore the precious sword and came to the Chancellor's mansion, where he asked where the Chancellor was. The attendant said, 'In the small chamber.' Cao went straight in. He saw Dong Zhuo sitting on his couch, with Lü Bu standing in attendance at his side. Zhuo said, 'Mengde, why so late?' Cao said, 'My horse is thin and slow.' Zhuo, turning to Bu, said, 'I have some fine horses lately presented from Xiliang; Fengxian, do thou go in person and pick one out to bestow upon Mengde.' Bu received the order and went. Cao silently said to himself, 'This traitor ought to die!' and was about to draw his sword and stab him. But fearing Zhuo's great strength, he dared not move lightly. Zhuo, being fat and large, could not endure sitting long; he therefore turned his body and lay down, with his face toward the inner wall. Cao thought again, 'The traitor's hour is come!' and swiftly drew the precious sword in his hand. Just as he was about to stab, unexpectedly Dong Zhuo, looking up into his dressing mirror, caught sight of Cao Cao behind him drawing the sword; he hastily turned his body and asked, 'Mengde, what dost thou?'
paragraphs.rhyme:
Next morn, [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) the precious sword had bound,
And to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s high hall his way he found.
He ask'd: 'Where stays my Lord?' Reply: 'Within
The inner chamber.' [Cao](char-cao-cao) straight enter'd in.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) saw [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) upon his couch awake,
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) beside, in service for his sake.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): '[Mengde](char-cao-cao), late?' [Cao](char-cao-cao): 'Slow my thinning horse.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) turn'd to [Bu](char-lu-bu): 'Of [Xiliang](loc-xiliang)'s recent course
Of fine new horses, sent to me of late,
[Fengxian](char-lu-bu), in person choose [Mengde](char-cao-cao) a mate.'
[Bu](char-lu-bu) took the charge, and from the chamber sped.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) silent thought: 'This traitor must lie dead!'
He reach'd to draw — but fear'd [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s giant strength,
And dar'd not move; held back his hand at length.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), fat and large, could not on couch long stay;
He turn'd, lay down, his face on inward way.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) thought: 'The traitor's hour is come at last!'
Swift drew the Sev'n-Star Sword and held it fast.
Just as the stab he poised — in mirror glass,
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) saw behind him [Cao](char-cao-cao) with blade in pass.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) turn'd back, his startl'd voice up-broke:
'[Mengde](char-cao-cao), what dost thou now?' — abrupt he spoke.

paragraphs.original: 時呂布已牽馬至閣外，操惶遽，乃持刀跪下曰：「操有寶刀一口，獻上恩相。」卓接視之，見其刀長尺餘，七寶嵌飾，極其鋒利，果寶刀也；遂遞與呂布收了。操解鞘付布。卓引操出閣看馬。操謝曰：「借願試一騎。」卓就教與鞍轡。操牽馬出相府，加鞭望東南而去。布對卓曰：「適來曹操似有行刺之狀，及被喝破，故推獻刀。」卓曰：「吾亦疑之。」
paragraphs.prose: At that time Lü Bu had already led the horse to outside the chamber. Cao, alarmed, then knelt down with the sword in his hands, saying, 'I have a precious sword, and present it to my benefactor-lord.' Zhuo took it and looked: he saw the sword was over a chi long, set with seven jewels inlaid, and exceedingly sharp — truly a precious sword. He thereupon handed it to Lü Bu to keep. Cao loosed the scabbard and gave it to Bu. Zhuo led Cao out of the chamber to look at the horse. Cao thanked him, saying, 'I would beg to try a ride.' Zhuo at once gave him saddle and bridle. Cao led the horse out of the Chancellor's mansion, applied the whip, and went off toward the southeast. Bu said to Zhuo, 'Just now Cao seemed to have the look of an assassin; when he was found out, he made a pretext of presenting the sword.' Zhuo said, 'I also suspected as much.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) had brought the steed without the door.
[Cao](char-cao-cao), fright, with sword in hand he knelt to floor:
'A treasure-sword I have — pray be it sent
Unto my benefactor-lord's content.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) took, and view'd: a chi or more in length,
With seven jewels set, of edge and strength,
Indeed a precious blade. He pass'd the blade aside
To [Bu](char-lu-bu) for keeping; [Cao](char-cao-cao) slipped sheath from side
And gave it too. [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) led [Cao](char-cao-cao) forth to view
The horse. [Cao](char-cao-cao) thank'd: 'A ride I'd try anew.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) bade them yield him saddle, bit, and rein.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) led the steed outside, nor turn'd again;
Apply'd the whip; south-eastward swift went he.
[Bu](char-lu-bu) said to [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo): 'Just now methought to see
[Cao](char-cao-cao) planning stroke; thy voice the act undid,
He turn'd to sword-gift, what was plotting hid.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) answer'd: 'I, too, doubted of his way.'
Within both hearts suspicion held its sway.

paragraphs.original: 正說話間，適李儒至，卓以其事告之。儒曰：「操無妻小在京，只獨居寓所。今差人往召，如彼無疑而便來，則是獻刀；如推託不來，則必是行刺，便可擒而問也。」卓然其說，即差獄卒四人往喚操。去了良久，回報曰：「操不曾回寓，乘馬飛出東門。門吏問之，操曰：『丞相差我有緊急公事』，縱馬而去矣。」儒曰：「操賊心逃竄，行刺無疑矣。」卓大怒曰：「我如此重用，反欲害我！」儒曰：「此必有同謀者，待拏住曹操便可知矣。」卓遂令遍行文書，畫影圖形，捉拏曹操。擒獻者，賞千金，封萬戶侯；窩藏者同罪。
paragraphs.prose: Just as they were speaking, Li Ru arrived; Zhuo told him of the matter. Ru said, 'Cao has no wife or children in the capital, but lives alone in his lodgings. Send now a man to summon him; if he come without misgiving, then it was indeed the presenting of a sword; but if he find some excuse and come not, then surely it was assassination — and you may seize and question him.' Zhuo found the words good, and sent four jailers at once to summon Cao. After a long while, they returned with the report, 'Cao did not return to his lodging; he mounted his horse and flew out of the east gate. The gate-officer asked him; Cao answered, "The Chancellor has charged me with urgent state business," and galloped away.' Ru said, 'The traitor Cao has fled with a guilty heart; that it was assassination is past doubt.' Zhuo, in great wrath, said, 'I trusted him so heavily, and he sought to harm me!' Ru said, 'There must be co-conspirators; once Cao is taken, we shall know.' Zhuo thereupon caused proclamations to be sent everywhere, drew up portraits and likenesses, to take Cao Cao. He who should seize and present him would receive a reward of a thousand jin of gold and the rank of Marquis of Ten Thousand Households; and any who should shelter him should be punished with the same crime.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Just as they spoke, [Li Ru](char-li-ru) came through the door,
And [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) rehearsed the thing that passed before.
[Ru](char-li-ru) said: '[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) has neither wife nor son
In capital — alone he hath his run.
Send now a man to summon him: if he
Come without doubt, his sword was all his plea;
But if pretext he find, refuse to come,
Then surely 'twas a stab — and we may sum
Him up, and question.' [Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) approved the plan,
And sent four jailers forth to fetch the man.
A long time pass'd; they came again, to say:
'[Cao](char-cao-cao) to his home came not; nay, on the way
He mounted horse and through the east gate flew.
The gate-guard ask'd; he answer'd: "Tasks anew
Of urgent state — the Lord hath set me ride,"
And gallop'd off — no more was [Cao](char-cao-cao) espy'd.'
[Ru](char-li-ru) said: '[Cao](char-cao-cao)'s flight declares the hidden plot:
The sword was no gift; thy life he sought.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), wroth: 'I trusted him in heavy use,
Yet he would strike at me — what foul abuse!'
[Ru](char-li-ru): 'Other plotters must support him; when
[Cao](char-cao-cao)'s caught, the rest shall stand reveal'd to ken.'
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) bade dispatch the edicts, wide and fast,
With portraits drawn — [Cao](char-cao-cao)'s face, his form, his cast;
Whoso should take and bring him, full reward,
A thousand jin of gold; he should be lord
As Marquis of Ten Thousand Households' style;
Whoso conceal'd him, like crime should defile.

paragraphs.original: 且說曹操逃出城外，飛奔譙郡。路經中牟縣，為守關軍士所獲，擒見縣令。操言：「我是客商，覆姓皇甫。」縣令熟視曹操，沈吟半晌，乃曰：「吾前在洛陽求官時，曾認得汝是曹操，如何隱諱？且把來監下，明日解去京師請賞。」把關軍士賜以酒食而去。
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of Cao Cao, who fled outside the city and flew toward Qiao Commandery. As he passed through Zhongmou County, he was taken by the soldiers who guarded the pass, who brought him before the county magistrate. Cao said, 'I am a traveling merchant; my surname is the double-character Huangfu.' The magistrate looked closely upon Cao, pondered a long while, and then said, 'When I was formerly in Luoyang in pursuit of office, I once knew you as Cao Cao — how is it that you would hide your name? For now take him into custody; tomorrow he shall be sent to the capital, that the reward may be claimed.' The pass-guards were given wine and food, and departed.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Now of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao), who fled the city's bound,
To Qiao Commandery, his native ground.
At Zhongmou County, on the road he pass'd,
The pass-guards seiz'd him, bound, and held him fast;
Before the County Magistrate he came.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) said: 'I am a merchant — Huangfu my name,
Two-character'd.' The Magistrate, with care,
Long view'd him, ponder'd; then declar'd him bare:
'When once in [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) I had sought for place,
I knew thee, [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) — wherefore wear false face?
Take him to gaol; the morn shall bring him forth,
Bound for the capital, to win the worth.'
The pass-guards, given gifts of food and wine,
Withdrew; [Cao](char-cao-cao) stay'd in prison's cold confine.

paragraphs.original: 至夜分，縣令喚親隨人暗地取出曹操，直至後院中審究；問曰：「我聞丞相待汝不薄，何故自取其禍？」操曰：「『燕雀安知鴻鵠志哉！』汝既拏住我，便當解去請賞。」縣令屏退左右，謂操曰：「汝休小覷我。我非俗吏，奈未遇其主耳。」操曰：「吾祖宗世食漢祿，若不思報國，與禽獸何異？吾屈身事卓者，欲乘間圖之，為國除害耳。今事不成，乃天意也！」縣令曰：「孟德此行，將欲何往？」操曰：「吾將歸鄉里，發矯詔，召天下諸侯興兵共誅董卓，吾之願也。」
paragraphs.prose: At midnight, the magistrate summoned his close attendants, and secretly brought Cao Cao out, leading him straight to the rear courtyard for examination. He asked, 'I hear that the Chancellor treated thee not poorly; why hast thou brought this calamity upon thyself?' Cao said, '"How can swallows and sparrows know the ambition of the great swan?" Since thou hast taken me, thou shouldst send me on to claim the reward.' The magistrate dismissed those at his side, and said to Cao, 'Slight me not. I am no common official; but I have not yet met with the proper master.' Cao said, 'My forefathers, generation upon generation, ate the salary of the Han; if I should not think to repay my country, how should I differ from the beasts? I have bowed myself to serve Zhuo, that I might seize an opportunity and plot against him, for the sake of removing the harm from the realm. Now the affair has failed — it is the will of Heaven!' The magistrate said, 'Mengde, on this journey, where wouldst thou go?' Cao said, 'I would return to my native village, issue a forged decree, and summon the nobles of the realm to raise troops together and execute Dong Zhuo: this is my wish.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
At midnight's hour the Magistrate his guard
Of trust then summon'd, brought [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) unbarr'd
Forth secret to the rear court; question'd there:
'I hear thy Lord hath treated thee with care,
Why bring such ruin to thy life?' [Cao](char-cao-cao) spake:
'The sparrow knows not what high swans undertake.
Thou hast me caught — then take me on with speed
To claim reward!' The Magistrate gave heed,
Dispers'd attendants, said: 'Slight me not so,
I am no common officer; I, though,
Have not yet met my master.' [Cao](char-cao-cao) replied:
'My forebears age by age the Han salt plied;
If I think not to pay back what I owe,
How differ I from beasts? [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s o'erthrow:
I plotted, bowing low to serve his pride;
For country's good, the harm to set aside.
Now is the deed undone — 'tis Heaven's will.'
Magistrate ask'd: 'Where dost thou journey still?'
[Cao](char-cao-cao): 'To my native village I shall fly,
Forge a decree, and call the lords on high
Throughout the realm, in arms with one assent,
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) to slay — this is my heart's intent.'

paragraphs.original: 縣令聞言，乃親釋其縛，扶之上坐，再拜曰：「公真天下忠義之士也！」曹操亦拜，問縣令姓名。縣令曰：「吾姓陳，名宮，字公臺。老母妻子，皆在東郡。今感公忠義，願棄一官，從公而逃。」操甚喜。是夜陳宮收拾盤費，與曹操更衣易服，各背劍一口，乘馬投故鄉來。
paragraphs.prose: The magistrate, hearing his words, personally loosed his bonds, helped him to a seat, bowed twice, and said, 'Sir, thou art truly a man of loyalty and righteousness in all the realm!' Cao Cao bowed in return, and asked the magistrate's name. The magistrate said, 'My surname is Chen, my given name Gong, my courtesy name Gongtai. My old mother, my wife, and my child are all in Dong Commandery. Now, being moved by your loyal righteousness, I would willingly abandon my office and flee with you.' Cao was greatly pleased. That very night Chen Gong gathered the traveling expenses, exchanged clothes with Cao, each bearing a sword on his back, and they mounted horses to set out for the home village.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The Magistrate, on hearing this, with hand
Of his own loos'd [Cao](char-cao-cao)'s bonds, and bade him stand
Bow'd twice, and said: 'Beneath the whole world's span,
Thou truly art a loyal, righteous man!'
[Cao](char-cao-cao) bow'd, and ask'd his name. The Lord replied:
'Chen is my surname; Gong my name supplied;
Gongtai my style. My mother, wife, and son
Within Dong comm'ndery dwell, every one.
Mov'd by thy loyal heart, I would forsake
This office, follow thee, and flight to make.'
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) was glad. That night [Chen Gong](char-chen-gong) made store
Of travel-coin; both donn'd new clothes they wore;
Each with a sword behind, on horse they laid
Their course was to [Cao](char-cao-cao)'s home; the way they made.

paragraphs.original: 行了三日，至成皋地方，天色向晚。操以鞭指林深處，謂宮曰：「此間有一人姓呂，名伯奢，是吾父結義弟兄；就往問家中消息，覓一宿，如何？」宮曰：「最好。」二人至莊前下馬，入見伯奢。奢曰：「我聞朝廷遍行文書，捉汝甚急，汝父已避陳留去了。汝如何得至此？」操告以前事，曰：「若非陳縣令，已粉骨碎身矣。」伯奢拜陳宮曰：「小姪若非使君，曹氏滅門矣。使君寬懷安坐，今晚便可下榻草舍。」說罷，即起身入內。良久乃出，謂陳宮曰：「老夫家無好酒，容往西村沽一樽來相待。」言訖，匆匆上驢而去。
paragraphs.prose: They travelled three days, and came to the region of Chenggao, when the daylight was drawing toward evening. Cao pointed with his whip to a place in the deep woods, and said to Gong, 'There lives here a man whose surname is Lü, named Boshe, a sworn brother of my father; let us go and ask after the news of my house, and seek a night's lodging — what say you?' Gong said, 'It is best.' The two came to the front of the manor, dismounted, and went in to see Boshe. Boshe said, 'I have heard that the court has issued proclamations everywhere, very urgent for thy capture; thy father has already retired to Chenliu. How didst thou come hither?' Cao told him what had passed, and said, 'Were it not for the magistrate of Chen, I should already be powdered bone and broken flesh.' Boshe bowed to Chen Gong, saying, 'If not for Your Honor, the house of Cao would be wiped out. Your Honor, set thy mind at ease and be seated; this night thou mayest lodge in our humble cottage.' Having spoken, he rose and went within. After a long while he came out, and said to Chen Gong, 'My old self has no good wine in the house; let me go to the western village to fetch a jar to entertain you.' With those words, he hastily mounted his donkey and went.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Three days they journey'd; to Chenggao came they,
As evening drew on, with day's last ray.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) with his whip the deep wood pointed near:
'Lü Boshe dwells here, sworn-brother held dear
Unto my father. Let's seek news of home,
And lodge a night within his rustic dome.'
[Gong](char-chen-gong): 'Best.' They to the manor came in span,
Dismounted, enter'd in to find the man.
Boshe: 'I heard the court hath edicts sent
For thy quick capture; and thy father went
Already to Chenliu, in flight from snare.
How com'st thou here?' [Cao](char-cao-cao) told the whole affair,
And said: 'But for Chen-County's lord, mine aid,
My bones were powder, all my body laid.'
Boshe to [Gong](char-chen-gong) then bow'd: 'If not for thee,
[Cao](char-cao-cao)'s house would all have perish'd utterly.
Lord, sit at ease; tonight thy rest may be
Beneath this humble cot, in courtesy.'
He spake, then in he went; long while to wait,
Came forth, and unto [Gong](char-chen-gong) he said: 'My state
Hath no good wine; let me west-village ride
And fetch a jar to entertain inside.'
He spoke; in haste he mounted ass, away,
And to the western village rode that day.

paragraphs.original: 操與宮坐久，忽聞莊後有磨刀之聲。操曰：「呂伯奢非吾至親，此去可疑，當竊聽之。」二人潛步入草堂後，但聞人語曰：「縛而殺之，何如？」操曰：「是矣！今若不先下手，必遭擒獲。」遂與宮拔劍直入，不問男女，皆殺之，一連殺死八口。搜至廚下，卻見縛一豬欲殺。宮曰：「孟德心多，誤殺好人矣！」急出莊上馬而行。行不到二里，只見伯奢驢鞍前　懸酒二瓶，手攜果菜而來，叫曰：「賢姪與使君何故便去？」操曰：「被罪之人，不敢久住。」伯奢曰：「吾已分付家人宰一豬相款，賢姪、使君何憎一宿？速請轉騎。」
paragraphs.prose: Cao and Gong sat long, when suddenly they heard the sound of knife-sharpening from behind the manor. Cao said, 'Lü Boshe is not my close kinsman; that he goes thus is suspicious — we should eavesdrop.' The two crept softly behind the thatch hall, where they heard a voice say, 'Bind and kill it — how say you?' Cao said, 'So it is! If we do not strike first, we shall surely be taken.' He thereupon drew his sword with Gong, went straight in, and asked nothing of male or female but slew all alike, killing eight in succession. They searched to the kitchen, and there saw a pig bound, ready to be slaughtered. Gong said, 'Mengde's heart is too suspicious — we have killed good people by mistake!' They hastily came out of the manor, mounted, and rode on. They had not gone two li when they saw Boshe with two bottles of wine hanging from his donkey's saddle, fruits and vegetables in his hand, calling out, 'Worthy nephew, Your Honor, why do you depart so soon?' Cao said, 'A man under sentence dares not abide long.' Boshe said, 'I have already given orders to my household to slaughter a pig in your honor; my nephew, Your Honor, why begrudge one night? Pray turn back at once.'
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Cao](char-cao-cao) and [Gong](char-chen-gong) sat long; from behind the place
A whetstone's grating broke the tranquil grace.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) said: 'Lü Boshe is no kin too near;
His leaving thus is strange — we should give ear.'
Both crept behind the thatch'd hall, soft of breath;
They heard within a voice: 'Bind first, give death —
How say'st thou?' [Cao](char-cao-cao): 'So 'tis! If we delay
And strike not first, we shall be ta'en their prey.'
[Cao](char-cao-cao) drew his sword, with [Gong](char-chen-gong); in haste they ran
And slew all there — both woman, child, and man.
Eight in succession fell. They search'd around
Unto the kitchen, where a pig was bound,
Awaiting slaughter. [Gong](char-chen-gong), observing, said:
'[Mengde](char-cao-cao) suspects too much; good folk lie dead!'
They hurried forth, took horse, and rode the road.
Not two li yet, when Boshe by them strode,
Two flasks of wine hung from his donkey's pack,
Fruits, herbs, in hand. He call'd to bring them back:
'Worthy nephew and Lord, why depart in haste?'
[Cao](char-cao-cao): 'Charged with crime, we cannot longer stay.'
Boshe: 'My household I have order'd send
A pig to slaughter — pray, my guest, attend!
Why grudge to lodge a single night?' he ask'd:
'Pray turn thy steed at once.' His words there pass'd.

paragraphs.original: 操不顧，策馬便行。行不數步，忽拔劍復回，叫伯奢曰：「此來者何人？」伯奢回頭看時，操揮劍砍伯奢於驢下。宮大驚曰：「適纔誤耳，今何為也？」操曰：「伯奢到家，見殺死多人，安肯干休？若率眾來追，必遭其禍矣。」宮曰：「知而故殺，大不義也！」操曰：「寧教我負天下人，休教天下人負我。」陳宮默然。
paragraphs.prose: Cao paid no heed, but whipped his horse and rode on. He had not gone many paces when suddenly he drew his sword, turned back, and cried to Boshe, 'Who is that coming yonder?' Boshe turned his head to look, and Cao swung his sword and cut Boshe down beneath his donkey. Gong, in great alarm, said, 'Just now was a mistake — what now is this?' Cao said, 'When Boshe reaches home and sees so many slain, will he be content to let it pass? If he leads his people in pursuit, we shall surely meet disaster.' Gong said, 'To know and yet to kill is great unrighteousness!' Cao said, 'Better that I betray all the men of the world, than that the men of the world betray me.' Chen Gong was silent.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Cao](char-cao-cao) heeded not, but whipp'd his steed and went.
Not many paces yet, with sudden bent,
Drew sword, turn'd back, and cried to Boshe near:
'Who comes there yonder?' Boshe turn'd to peer;
[Cao](char-cao-cao) swung his sword, and cut Boshe down dead;
From off his donkey to the ground he sped.
[Gong](char-chen-gong), alarm'd: 'A while back was a mistake;
But this — what dost thou now? For what's at stake?'
[Cao](char-cao-cao) said: 'Should Boshe home return and see
So many slain, would he in peace let be?
If he should lead his folk to chase our flight,
They'll seize us surely ere the fall of night.'
[Gong](char-chen-gong): 'Knowing, yet to kill — wrong most severe!'
[Cao](char-cao-cao): 'Better I betray the world's whole sphere,
Than let all under Heaven betray me here.'
[Chen Gong](char-chen-gong) was silent, not a word made clear.

paragraphs.original: 當夜行數里，月明中敲開客店門投宿。喂飽了馬，曹操先睡。陳宮尋思：「我將謂曹操是好人，棄官跟他；原來是個狠心之徒！今日留之，必為後患。」便欲拔劍來殺曹操。正是：設心狠毒非良士，操卓原來一路人。畢竟曹操性命如何，且聽下文分解。
paragraphs.prose: That night they travelled some li, and in the bright moonlight knocked at the door of an inn and took lodging. The horses being well fed, Cao Cao lay down first to sleep. Chen Gong pondered to himself, 'I had thought Cao Cao was a good man, and gave up my office to follow him; but he turns out to be a man of a cruel heart! If I keep him today, he will surely be a calamity hereafter.' And he was about to draw his sword and slay Cao Cao. As the verse runs: 'He whose heart sets cruel poison is no man of worth; / Cao and Zhuo, after all, are men of one same road.' What in the end shall become of Cao Cao's life — listen to the next chapter for the answer.
paragraphs.rhyme:
That night they rode some li; the moon shone bright;
They knock'd an inn-door, lodg'd there for the night.
The horses fed; [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) to slumber went.
[Chen Gong](char-chen-gong) sat thinking: 'I had judg'd [Cao](char-cao-cao) bent
To virtue good; I left my office post
To follow him — but now I count the cost:
A cruel-hearted man he proves to be!
If kept this day, he'll bring calamity.'
He rais'd his blade, intent [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) to slay;
Just so the verse this scene doth now display:
'A poison-cruel heart, no man of worth;
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao), [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) — one road they tread on earth.'
And what of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s life shall now befall,
The next chapter shall make it plain to all.
